cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: The haloed Christ stands in a red mantle between two great horned bulls that rear up and press against him on either side. The image follows the verse written above it: 'Many bulls have compassed me: strong bulls of Bashan have beset me round' — a prophecy read as the hostility surrounding Christ in his Passion.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:monumental-kanakaria-apse.summary: This photograph, taken before the theft of the mosaic, shows the Virgin seated frontally on a throne within an almond-shaped mandorla, holding the Christ Child on her lap; an archangel survives at the left, with areas of loss painted in during restoration. The image of Mother and Child enclosed in a glory of light is among the very few pre-Iconoclast apse mosaics surviving in the eastern Mediterranean.
facts: The mosaics were stolen from the church after 1975; some were sold on the art market in the United States, and after a lengthy legal battle (reported in 1989) they were returned to Cyprus and are displayed in the Byzantine Museum, Nicosia.
Around the edge of the apse were medallions of the apostles framed with acanthus; the mosaics are generally dated to the 6th century, contemporary with Ravenna's.

feat:benedictional-of-aethelwold-baptism.summary: Standing waist-deep in the swirling waters of the Jordan, Christ receives baptism from John while angels attend him and the dove of the Holy Spirit descends from heaven, all enclosed in a lush frame of gold bars and leafy acanthus. This luxurious book of blessings was made for Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester and a leader of the tenth-century monastic reform in England. It is the masterpiece of the Winchester School, the most splendid style of late Anglo-Saxon painting.
facts: A poem in the book records that Æthelwold commanded it to be written by a monk named Godeman, who may later have become abbot of Thorney.
It contains the solemn episcopal blessings pronounced at Mass on the feasts of the Church year, and some 28 full-page miniatures survive.
The exuberant acanthus frames combine Carolingian models with a distinctively English love of fluttering, energetic ornament.
The manuscript belonged for generations to the Dukes of Devonshire before the British Museum acquired it in 1957.

feat:egger-lienz-risen-christ-lienz.summary: A gaunt, beardless Christ sits half-length before an empty tomb, holding the banner of the Resurrection, his emaciated body marked by suffering rather than glorified. Egger-Lienz, who had witnessed the First World War as a war painter, made this stark figure the culmination of a four-part cycle in the district memorial chapel for the fallen of Lienz. It offers resurrection hope that does not look away from the cost of death.
facts: The unconventional image provoked fierce protests; on 5 May 1926 the Vatican placed the chapel under interdict, forbidding church services there for decades.
The press mocked the figure as 'consumptive'; the chapel was finally reconsecrated in June 1987. These are the only frescoes Egger-Lienz ever painted.
Egger-Lienz himself is buried in the chapel, which was dedicated on 8 September 1925 and designed by the architect Clemens Holzmeister.
